utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ierace, is it Mr. Stamp who's going to continue or...?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Mr. Stamp will continue for approximately 20 minutes, and then I will do the remaining part of our oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be approximately a little bit less than an hour then. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. President. Good morning to all. Yesterday, we were discussing incident 3 -- 5, five children were killed, and Witness AI and other children, including the Witness Todorovic, were wounded in front of 4 Clara Cetkin Street. That is the two southernmost impact sites. The other 82-millimetre round fell a little bit over 100 metres to the north of that along Osrenska Street and killed one child and wounded three others. In the Prosecution's closing brief, it has already been argued that it is clear that the two 120-millimetre rounds were fired first, and that is what caused the children and Witness AI to run towards the entrances. The Court invited and we will not show it now -- but the Court has invited to show Exhibits 3281F, that is a video with Todorovic showing where he and the other children were playing, and the route they took to run to the building at Klara Cetkin Street. And that could be reviewed in juxtaposition with Exhibit 3281G, which is a video in which the witness Kapetanovic showed the investigator where that group ran from. And the Court can get an idea as to the distance the kids would have to run, especially having regard to the fact that they were running through snow. There was snow on the ground and they were indeed sledding that day. Consider, coupled with that, the fact that Witness AI heard the two 120-millimetre rounds falling somewhere within Alipasino Polje before they started to run. What that indicates is that it is possibly probable that the mission of the 120-millimetre is not necessarily the same as that of the 82-millimetres. Indeed, the fact that Witness AI did not hear the 120-millimetre being round fired indicated that they were fired from some distance further behind the 82-millimetre rounds, as is evidence in 120-millimetre mortar round can fire over a distance of 120 metres -- I beg your pardon. Over a distance of 6.500 metres. What then was the purpose of the two 82-millimetre rounds? It is submitted this was simply a furtherance of a policy of random fire into areas where civilians were expected to be. The Court will have to assess the fact that the two 82-millimetre rounds fell in front of the two apartments buildings where people, anybody there, children, whatever citizens were there, would have been expected to be escaping sometime after hearing the explosion of the 120-millimetre rounds. If one 82-millimetre mortar fired, then it would mean that the mortar would have had to be relayed from one entry to another entry. If two 82 millimetre mortar fired, then the question arises: What level of coincidence it is that these two separate mortar barrels would fire and hit at approximately the same time in that particular set of circumstances two entrances along those two roads? It is submitted that the reasonable inference, the only reasonable inference, is that the entry to the buildings was the target, and the persons who fired knew that persons would be escaping towards those entries. And on this particular occasion, there were very, very tragic consequences. In respect to incident 4, that is a very clear incident. It is an incident in which General Rose said that evidence quite clearly indicated that the citizens gathered for rations were deliberately targeted by the Bosnian Serb army. It bears reiterating that the three 120-millimetre rounds fell in a radius of 40 metres. The evidence in respect of the firing of mortars and artillery is that the firing can be corrected, and correction means moving the barrel to get it on a target. If the three rounds fell within such a small radius, it is clear evidence as General Rose suggested that this area where the civilians gathered was the target. Interestingly, as far as that incident is concerned, the two 120-millimetre mortar rounds that fell on the ground, lodged and penetrated the ground to quite a significant agree, one of them actually shattered the ground. The other one can be seen in video D64. And the interesting thing is that nobody has raised any issue about the fact that this round was lodged in the concrete surface. And it would be interesting to compare the video in respect to that round and the video in respect of the Markale incident where so many complaints have been raised. If that video D64 -- and this is just a short extract from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the mortar fin lodged in the concrete surface. I should point out that I think the translation of the report says asphalt surface, but it is quite clear from the photographs and the video that that children's playground where the people were gathered to buy the flour that was delivered with the humanitarian aid rations was a concrete surface. We could perhaps have a look at Exhibit P2279A, which is a video in respect of the round -- well, not the round, the stabiliser fin lodged in the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Interestingly we see being excavated by an UNPROFOR member with a knife. It could be stopped now. Thank you. Although we're not aware, it has not been in evidence as to the exact quality of the concrete and the exact quality of the asphalt in Markale and the exact compaction of the dirt or soil beneath, the videos and the pictures of those two are relatively similar, and no complaint is made in respect to incident 4. Indeed, not only General Rose had that incident -- for -- with a clear example of targeting, without expressing any concern about the lodgement of the stabiliser fin so deeply into the concrete surface, but the experts who examined the scene of the impact at Markale, and this includes Sabljica, Cavcic, Zecevic, Hamill, and five other experts specifically brought together for this investigation because of their expertise. All of them, the Bosnian experts, the international experts, all of them that examined the crater at Markale determined that it had been fired by 120-millimetre mortar, fired in a conventional manner from a mortar tube, that it exploded with an impact on the surface, not an underground explosion, there's no issue as to the round penetrating and then exploding. None of them expressed any surprise or concern or any issue as to how far this stabiliser fin lodged. This was something that had been experienced clearly of all of them. The first time, apparently, that we're hearing that one can use formulas to say "it couldn't have happened" is probably in this trial. There have been arguments raised in respect to the photographs of the fragments that were recovered. These were photographs D60 and D61, which we could have a look at quickly. It was said that they are two diameters indicated in the semi-circular parts of the fragments, and it is also said that some of them indicate that there are different sized threading. A review of Exhibit P3806, which is on the screen now, which is a cross-section showing the interior of the fuse shows that within the fuse, there are many subsystems which are connected by screw fittings of differing diameters with different-sized threading. The result of the explosion is that the entire system is stretched, becomes warped, and it smashes into the ground. Nothing in Exhibits D60 or D61 is inconsistent Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with the Prosecution's case. The Chamber is also invited to have a look at P3802 which is a photograph of the fragmentation of a mortar shell. One will see that in the middle of the circular fragments, the pieces are a little bit more chunky, I would say, than those going to one side of the round. And to the left of the photograph, you'll see at the top the bits look like a little bit more like shards while those at the bottom are more like the pictures in the middle. That middle part, the chunkier piece, is consistent with the Prosecution's case. Because according to Dr. Vilicic and Dr. Besic, the front ogival part of the 120-millimetre mortar round, an explosion on contact, blasts away forming a crater. The crime-scene technician Besic said that he found the fragment in the crater. So it would be expected that these chunkier pieces which are part of the front ogival part of the round with what is found in the crater. And every shape that you see in D61 and D62 you can find among the shapes of these rounds in the middle of the standard fragments from mortar rounds. Of course, the shardier rounds from the side -- I beg your pardon, the shardier fragments, the sharper, longer fragments from the side of the round, those are the fragments which are emitted, and those fragments that of course be lodged in the bodies of the victims would have been washed away with the blood and gore. So when appraised in its totality, the evidence in respect of the Markale incident is manifestly clear. Even the Defence witness, the Defence expert agrees on fundamental matters which support a clear inference that it was fired from Mrkovici. But that is not all. The Prosecution had brought direct evidence of persons who were close to the line in the direction of fire, that are close to the Sharpstone feature area. Witness AK heard it being fired. Admittedly, she heard sounds over her house shortly after she heard it being fired, and she associated those sounds with the round travelling over her house. It is, of course, impossible for her to hear the sound of the round travelling over her house. So whatever she heard over her house is not associated with the sound, or not associated with the mortar, the flight of the mortar as it passed over her house. But the fact is she did hear it fire. And if Exhibit 3666 is reviewed, one could see the exact location of her house in respect to that part of the confrontation line along the line of fire. More interestingly is evidence of Witness AF who had been a combatant, was very, very familiar with the sound of mortars firing, more so than the average citizen of Sarajevo. He had been retired because of personal difficulties. And he was in his mother's backyard which was located about 200 metres from the confrontation line. And that area is shown in Exhibit P3668 which is a map on which he marked the approximate location of the line and -- I'm told that it is protected. However, I don't think the information on it would cause any difficulties because all the names have been -- there is no name indicated on the map. So perhaps we could proceed without going into closed session. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I have the exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Exhibit P3668. And I believe it was shown in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What often happened, and we were confronted with that yesterday as well is that when a document was shown in open court, sometimes parts of it were invisible because they have been yellow stickers on it. So before we look at it, I would first like to check that there's nothing on it. Sometimes the names are...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have ensured that the names are not on this part of it which we are going to show now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the other thing I'd like to check is whether it's really the name that's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I think I could proceed without it. I would invite the Court to have a look at where he placed the house in respect to the confrontation, and also to have a look at Exhibit 3131 which is a set of photographs of the area of his house in relation to where the confrontation line was. One would see that there was no obstacle or impediment for his hearing the sound of a mortar being fired from beyond the line. The Witness Higgs did say that the UNMOs use their ears to determine where the mortar fire was coming from. I beg your pardon, it was Hamill who said. Higgs added quite reasonably that sound can be deflected. That is why incident 1, as we explained in the brief, we do not rely on Witness...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was indicating in incident 3, we would not rely on Witness AI's testimony solely because there were buildings between where he was and the firing point. We rely on the evidence which excludes the possibility that it could have been fired anywhere between where it landed and the confrontation line. And also the evidence of the ballistic examiners who established the direction of fire. However, in respect of the Markale incident, the circumstances are quite different. Witness AF was located at such a position that there's nothing which one could objectively say would have interfered with an accurate assessment of where the mortar was fired from. If I could quickly move on to a different area, with your leave, Mr. President, the Defence in its brief made a number of references, it has submitted misleading references, to the casualty figures that were evidenced in the expert statement of Ewa Tabeau, and as it was amplified in her testimony. The basic data regarding civilian casualties are summarised in paper 1 of page 4, and the figures show that in every part of Sarajevo there was a confrontation line. And throughout the whole of the indictment period, notwithstanding certain laws, usually as a result of international pressure, civilians were being killed and wounded on a daily basis. One can glean that from the annexes to the expert statement. While the majority of those killed were men, many children, women, and elderly were reported among casualties as well. Among those killed, there were 295 children, 670 women, 85 elderly. Incidentally, yesterday we heard that within the Bosnian government lines, 1.185 civilians were killed, and 4.701 were wounded. Actually, those figures are the numbers only for those who were killed by shelling and sniping respectively. It is said that the ratio of men to women killed was 83 per cent to 17 per cent, and it is argued that this ratio is inconsistent with the Prosecution's case. This is a ratio for the overall total of killed persons, most of whom are soldiers, and very few of these soldiers were women. Among the civilians were killed, if one looks at that specific subgroup, the civilians killed, the ratio is 55 per cent men, and 45 per cent women. These figures indicate generally speaking that there was random targeting of the civilians. The Defence also at paragraph 703 and 704 of the closing brief calculated that there were only 100 civilian deaths in 1994, and argue that this figure rebuts an inference of a campaign of targeting civilians. The contrary is true. Table A 3.13 of the annexes to Tabeau's expert statements records that in 1994, a total of 179 civilians were killed with 146 of them occurring in the first two months. The evidence discloses a reason for the dramatic fall in the rate of killings after February 1994, which is the month of the Markale incident when international pressure was brought to bear. And in the same vein, the evidence also reveals the reason for the decrease in the rate of civilian casualties over the indictment period. In fact the evidence is, and I think that was part of the homework of Ewa Tabeau, that the rates started to decline after a few months of the war, even before the tenure of the accused began. And the reason from the evidence clearly is that as the conflict dragged on, the survivor skills of the residents became more and more acutely refined as a result of the rigorous lessons taught by past traumatic experiences of the campaign. They organised more effectively and employed a variety of measures progressively improved over time to protect themselves, like barriers at night, building trenches and barricades for safe passage, and putting schools and performing religious Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rites in basements. Some of them even lived in their basements for months, coming out just to fetch the basic necessities of life. Mustafa Kovac, the chief of the civil defence, testified that these protective measures, the barricades erected in places deemed to be dangerous based on the number of casualties and the frequency of shooting in the past led to a significant decrease in the casualties. In any case, it is reiterated here that the Prosecution's case is not that the aim was to kill and injure as many Sarajevans as possible, it was primarily to terrorise the population in furtherance of political objectives. May it please you, Mr. President, I would like to stop here. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. I would take this opportunity to explain why I was a bit cautious about showing any maps, because apart from names, sometimes witnesses marked elements that would -- could be a clue to the place where they lived, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. I realise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I might start by picking up on the last point made by Mr. Stamp. In the evidence is a map marked by Mlada Halili indicating the route that she and her husband and mother took on the day that her mother was killed. She explained that it was a route used by Sarajevans to avoid as much as possible places in the city which were exposed to sniper fire. A well-used route. The map is of poor quality, but the marking is quite distinct. And that's quite helpful in understanding one of the measures taken by civilians to protect themselves. Yesterday, at the time I sat down, I had been making some submissions in relation to the matchbox fire. The fire chief, Mr. Jusufovic placed that as having occurred at Dolac Malta. Both men, van Lynden and Jusufovic said that men, women, and children, all civilians, made their way as best they could out of the building. Jusufovic pointed out the lower levels were also set ablaze by the incendiary rounds, and when they attempted to use the fire brigade extension ladder, the firefighters were shot at. The Defence in relation to this incident at paragraph 807 said: "Baron van Lynden declared not being able to dismiss that this building would have been used prior to the attacks for sniper fires. This only mentioned by a war journalist means that in all likelihood, it was more than a probability." In other words, the Defence seeks to justify the attack on the basis that it was used by snipers. Firstly, that misstates the evidence of Baron van Lynden. When cross-examined about that use, he said it was a theoretical possibility. He was convinced that it had not been used for military purposes. But even assuming it had been, it would grossly offend the principle of proportionality to jeopardise so many civilian lives, lives of men, women, and children, in order to burn out the highest residential building in Sarajevo, because it had been used by snipers. That assumes, but there is no evidence of, namely, that it was used by snipers. Mr. President, if we could move into private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So that is consistent with the evidence of Witness D as the source of fire being precisely on the line of houses occupied by snipers who were equipped with night sights just to the north of Osrenska Street. If we please now go to the next slide. We have that it on the screen, I think. Mr. President, here we see Dr. Radinovic's map for Grbavica. One will notice the large number of white circles marked by the Prosecution as being pre-indictment. We see two entries for number 44. The foundational documents for those entries indicate that the target, in fact, should be in Vogosca, Hum, and Ogoska. There is no explanation as to why they appear in Marin Dvor and Novo Sarajevo. One also notices two number 49s which are references to boundaries of areas of responsibility with no explanation as to why they appear where they do. We see two entries numbered 19. In fact there are four entries for number 19 on the map as a whole, and of course I'm referring to various entries here which have not been marked white. Next slide, please. This is a portion of Kucanin's map of Grbavica. Next slide. The yellow arrow indicates a position which Mr. Kucanin indicated as a constant source of sniper fire against civilians during the indictment period. He described it as being a line of four skyscrapers 15 storeys each. One can see that it is along the banks of the Miljacka River which was indeed the confrontation line at that stage. A comparison with the maps marked by John Ashton indicates they are the very same skyscrapers in which he was shown around in which he saw thousands of spent shells. A comparison with the maps of Witness D indicates again, they are the same four skyscrapers that were gathered by Witness D's platoon from which he observed snipers entering and leaving. Baron van Lynden gave evidence that he went into skyscrapers in the same area. And indeed, alongside this block of four to the left -- to the west is another block of four. And in those skyscrapers, the ones that were entered by Baron van Lynden, he not only saw dummies being erected, he not only saw walkie-talkies being used by spotters for the snipers, but also saw the professional snipers with optical sights. From that block of four alongside this block, the Prosecution says Milada Halili's mother was shot. It is important to remember the use of spotters, the use of telescopes, the use of walkie-talkies in considering whether civilians shot as they emerged from behind containers or shot from under trucks containing containers were hit from those known sources deliberately. Van Lynden visited these blocks with a military police escort provided personally by General Mladic in late September, 1992. Therefore, there can be no doubt that these professional snipers operating in the first three weeks of the accused's tenure were doing so as part of the SRK. One and a half years later, Colonel Fraser in the closing months of the accused's tenure described how the snipers operating from Grbavica would in a morning ritual hit telegraph poles to indicate to the hundreds of French troops trying to locate them that they were in position and ready for action. And there, they would wait each day for the civilians, including children, according to Colonel Fraser, to appear. Colonel Fraser made clear he was referring to sniper alley, Marsal Tito Boulevard, and only civilians used it. A moment's reflection on that, if one considers day in and day out for a year and a half, these snipers operated from Grbavica, it could only have happened when one considers the link to General Mladic in September 1992 that the accused wanted it, intended it to happen. Next slide -- go back one, please. Another aspect of this map by Kucanin is the numbers 6, 7, and 8 which appear in a marked area above the yellow area. He said there were three snipings of trams that he investigated in the indictment period. I will come back to that. Next slide. This is a photograph taken by John Ashton from Marin Dvor looking south, and we see squarely in the middle of the photograph the Jewish cemetery which the Prosecution has called evidence to the effect was the source - SRK positions on the Jewish cemetery - of considerable fire against civilians in Marin Dvor in central Sarajevo. In this photograph, we see the chapel at the bottom of the cemetery. Cemetery behind it. And if one visually places over that image the evidence as to the position, the undisputed evidence as to the position of the SRK lines, it was agreed by both sides that certainly, they were at the top of the cemetery and certainly they were to the right of the cemetery as we view it. This makes the point, this photograph, that even if the SRK were not operating from the chapel, it didn't matter, because from above the chapel, from the southern boundary of the cemetery where they were located, they had a clear line of fire into the city. Next image, please. Here I now switch given the shortness of time to incidents 11 and 2 which occurred at the Skenderija. The Prosecution says that the source of fire was a feature known as Baba rock. This is the sniping map for incident 11 marked by General Karavelic in dark blue to indicate the forward confrontation line of SRK positions. He placed that line through Baba rock, and he also in so doing followed the road, the road from Lukavica to Pale. The Defence witnesses said "no, that's not right. The front-line position was to the south of the road. They didn't hold the road, therefore, they didn't hold Baba rock, and therefore they could not have been responsible." They said "Baba rock was in neutral territory, was in no-man's-land." Even if it was, it makes no different. The fact that snipers operate from no-man's-land as opposed to confrontation lines is not a problem. Second point I wish to make is that the evidence is in support of the Prosecution proposition. If we go to the next map, we see here a map marked by John Ashton of the same area. If one looks at the squiggly road towards the centre of the map, and then we go back to the last image one can see, if one looks carefully in the centre of this map, the same squiggly road. In order to get an understanding that these two maps cover the same area. Back to the Ashton map, please. Ashton marked this road because he said it was the route he took when he travelled from Lukavica to Pale, and he was doing that at the time of incidents 2 and 11. How was he able to travel on a road on SRK territory, initially venture into no-man's-land, continue driving south to Pale, and then back again. That doesn't make sense. The only way he could have done that was if the road was in SRK territory. Mrs. Basara Karavic [phoen] gave evidence that the road actually passed between the two rock features, so you had rocks on one side of the road and then rocks on the other. The issue arose partly because General Karavelic didn't mark map number 2 the same way that he marked map number 11. He was shown map number 2 first and then marked map number 11, giving rise to that inconsistency. It was clearly an oversight. Next map. Another issue in relation to incident number 2 was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. whether there were any legitimate targets. This is a map marked by defence witness. If one looks at the circle placed near the name Sirokaca, one sees a multiple road junction and immediately to the right of it a circle. A witness said that was a school building that was used by artillery units. The position of incident number 2 is to the left. One sees a road going up the screen from behind the letters RO. And then as we follow it up, it forks. The position of number 2 was to -- a little higher and to the left of that fork. In other words, some 200 metres from the position of the school. Next map, please. This is Dr. Radinovic's map of the area. We see there is only one military target he has identified anywhere near incident 2 or incident 11, 148. He based it on a pre-indictment reference. Well it didn't exist at the time of incident 2. But even if it did, keeping in mind that the circles that he used had a diameter of some 200 metres, when one looks at the scale on these maps, it is quite misleading. In other words, in relation to both incidents, there were no nearby military targets that could be relevant to the incidents themselves. Next slide, please. Now, Mrs. Basara Karavic described the source of fire as being Baba rock or Ozmici [phoen]. And there was a little un -- lack of clarity in relation to what she quite meant. Was she saying that Baba rock was also known as Ozmici or were they different place. To a degree, it didn't matter, because she said both places were in SRK territory, enemy territory, and both were sources of fire. If one goes through the evidence looking for other references to Ozmici, one again comes back to investigator Kucanin who marked on his map in position number 2 Ozmici, which he described as being one of the highest sources of fire into the city against civilians during the indictment period. Again, we see the squiggly road just beneath the 2 which helps us to position where Ozmici was, and it happens to be where Baba rock was as he has marked it. Next map, please. This is Dr. Radinovic's map for Sedrenik, where we had two incidents, 3 and 8. Sharpstone to the top left. First observation, and perhaps the only one I need to make in the time I have is that none of these targets are anywhere near the relevant incident positions. The same could be said for his map in relation to incidents 16 and 17. There were no military targets marked anywhere near them. I'll leave these slides at this stage with just one more, if we could have that. The Defence in its written submissions complained that for all the evidence of funerals being shelled, we saw no photographs of such a thing. And said that if there had been a photograph taken at the time that a funeral was shelled, that would be helpful. Here is such photograph taken by journalist Vaal. You will recall his evidence, that he took this photograph of a woman gathering wood, and in the background one sees Kosevo Hospital. In the middle ground, he explained, there's a funeral procession entering the line of symmetry. He explained that seconds after he took this photograph, it was shelled, and the funeral procession scattered. He wanted to run, the woman wouldn't. He spoke to her and asked her to accompany him to safety, but she wouldn't. She had a totally fatalistic attitude by that stage about survival. If the Defence wishes to see further images in relation to funerals, we also have the series of photographs taken by the UN military observer who investigated the shelling of a funeral at Lion cemetery where some of the funeral attendees sought refuge in the then-abandoned premises of PAPA 3 when a 24-year-old woman was hit by a mortar as she tried to enter the front door. Mr. President, that completes the images for the moment, returning now to some other matters -- going to some other matters I should say. In their written submissions, the Defence stated that the scheduled sniping incidents were not protested to the accused, thereby inferring that the accused was deprived of an opportunity to investigate each incident. But if the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the accused was, at his level of senior command, in fact ordering the campaign, failure to inform him of these individual incidents is inconsequential. Consistent with the Prosecution thesis, the accused we have heard evidence failed to investigate any of the multitude of protests in relation to the sniping of civilians that were made to him personally and also through his liaison staff which existed in that part for that very purpose, for receiving protests. Bergeron, who was the UN commander from April 1993 to April 1994 gave evidence that he regularly met with the accused, and he personally protested to the accused through that 12-month period the sniping of men, women, and children civilians by the SRK forces. So there, out of the 23 months, is 12. Colonel Fraser who commenced his period in April 1994 when General Bergeron finished said that protests were made from then right through to the end of the accused's tenure. And at that stage, increasingly in relation to specific incidents. But Colonel Indic admitted to this Trial Chamber from the witness box that not one solitary incident of the shooting of a civilian was ever investigated by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Shooting of the UN was a different matter. The accused would investigate those. So we see that he would investigate when he was motivated to do so. The explanation offered by Colonel Indic as to why the shooting of civilians was never investigated, that they didn't have sufficient information, is totally lacking in credibility. Indeed, we saw that there were admissions at a lower level by the SRK, that they were engaged in the business of sniping. We have in evidence a UN SITREP dated the 13th of July, 1994, issued through the headquarters of General Van Baal noting that the battalion commander responsible for the territory of the home for the blind in Nedzarici admitted the SRK was sniping from it and promised "that there would be no more sniping from that place." The date of that admission was four weeks before the accused was replaced, nine months after the shooting of Faruk Hrncic [phoen] in his father's truck, four months after Franjic Greguric [phoen] was shot, and three weeks after the shooting of Senalja Meritenovic [phoen], the 16 year old sholt as she crossed the road, all from the house for the blind. I mentioned trams earlier. Conspicuous by its complete absence from the Defence case, and its written submissions, was any justification for the targeting of trams. Indeed, the accused could hardly justify that behaviour. Implicit in this blanket omission from the Defence case is by inference a concession to the Prosecution submission that it was without any justification at all. And yet, the evidence establishes not only that such acts were perpetrated by SRK soldiers, but that it was ordered at the level of the SRK and VRS leadership. I refer, of course, to the evidence of General Van Baal who was informed by the chief of staff of the VRS, General Milovanovic, that if the UN succeeded in getting the trams running in Sarajevo, they would be targeted. General Rose said it was of great symbolical importance to get the trams running again in the aftermath of Markale and that this was achieved by April 1994. And General Milovanovic was as good as his word; the trams were targeted. Incident 24, for instance, occurred two months after the trams were restarted. In June 1994, a tram passing through Marin Dvor was shot, persons injured. General Rose also said that he had "a memory of a suspicion at the time that a Bosnian government sniper team may have fired on one of the trams." This serves to illustrate the issue of whether the Bosnians could have been responsible for the crimes committed against the civilians and not the accused. In my opening of the Prosecution case, I said that the commission of crimes were not confined to one side in this conflict. And indeed, we have heard evidence, such as that from General Rose, that there were indications that Bosnians may have been responsible for some isolated incidents against their own civilians. So what is the relevance of this evidence in this trial in relation to this accused? Taking the evidence at its highest, assuming hypothetically it occurred, the bare fact that the accused was not the only one committing such crimes is of no assistance to him in his defence Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at all. It could only be relevant if it created a reasonable doubt that it was not the accused's subordinates who were responsible for perpetrating these offences. However, the evidence that the Prosecution relies upon that the accused's subordinates did commit the crimes charged and that he ordered it is not contingent upon disproving Bosnian perpetrations as well. I refer in particular to the evidence of eyewitness accounts of the sources of fire, where eyewitnesses have seen the shells, the muzzles of the guns firing on SRK territory, the observations of UN military observers in the Lima positions alongside the mortar units, the artillery places, watching the shells laying indiscriminately in the city, watching the mortars being kicked and then fired, Witness D watching drunking crews operating mortars, and the evidence of admissions made at all times level of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the VRS, and threats and threats carried out. None of that depends at all on disproving perpetrators on the Bosnian side. It's quite independent. It's also pertinent in this regard to observe that time and again, the witnesses called by the Prosecution who gave evidence that there were indications that the Bosnians may have been responsible for some isolated incidents against their own civilians were the very same witnesses who gave the most damning evidence against the accused. Patrick Henneberry is one example who comes to mind. There are others. There was no inconsistency in their minds and in their evidence with the guilt of the accused. He also demonstrated, incidentally, the impartiality of those witnesses. So it's not a question of either the accused or the Bosnians being responsible, but rather whether the Bosnians as well as the accused bore some responsibility for civilian casualties. And again, importantly, there was no evidence that fire from one part of Bosnian territory to another part of Bosnian territory resulted in significant casualties. If it happened, the scale was small, and that observation was made by a number of senior UN witnesses. I emphasise that my argument on this point assumes that some on the Bosnian side did perpetrate such crimes. It was not that conclusive. Richard Gray was a tragic figure. His evidence lacked credibility for a number of reasons, some of which at least went beyond his control. The Defence played an interview with a person who related the shooting of a soldier by Bosnians, but they did not call him to give evidence, to be tested under cross-examination, or even to explain where his information came from. To return now to the subject of the sniping of the trams. Rose said there was a suspicion that one tram was shot by Bosnian snipers, a suspicion. That does not detract from the evidence that the trams were shot on multiple occasions by the SRK and that Milovanovic effectively admitted it by threatening it and carrying it out. To give another example in relation to Kosevo Hospital, our written submissions detail the analysis of shell impacts on the hospital in December 1992 and January 1993. We heard evidence from Cutler and from Harding of the detailed analysis carried out, the type of shells that were used that were not possessed by the ABiH, but we also heard evidence from Hamill who said that 12 months later, on the 5th of December, 1993, he was passing through Kosevo Hospital and he looked at an impact site we he deduced to be a tank shell and he formed the opinion that it was not fired from the area under the control of the SRK but, rather, fired from within the city. He formed this impression, he said, from what he saw on the spot, not a complete analysis. But assuming it was true, assuming that there had been a complete analysis, which there wasn't, and that it was fired from within the city, that does not detract at all from the evidence of Cutler and Harding in relation to what happened 12 months before, 11 months before, in December 1992 and January 1993. It's not either/or; it's as well as. This has some relevance also to the issue of terror. The terror count is the charge which best captures the criminality of the accused partly because it puts in context all of the other charges and identifies the true victims, namely, the civilian population as a whole. If some on the Bosnian side shot or shelled their own, or paramilitaries fought each other on the Bosnian side, in the same fashion as with the other charges the accused is not relieved of responsibility for his actions. The Defence argument, in other words, is built on a false premise, again, assuming for the sake of the argument that civilians were in fact terrorised by Bosnian actions and the war experience generally. As Dr. Turner noted terror can be a response to more than one stimulus factor. Put simply, if the evidence establishes that the objective of the campaign undertaken by the accused was indeed to terrorise the civilian population and if the evidence also establishes that the civilian population were terrorised by the sniping and shelling from the SRK side, it doesn't matter that they also experienced terror as a result of living so close to an armed conflict in terms of its legitimate aspects. It doesn't matter that they also felt terror as a result of fighting -- infighting between paramilitaries, and it doesn't matter that some of the sniping and some of the shelling didn't come from the SRK side, if that was established, which it is not. Terror does not have to have one source. Yesterday, I made submissions in relation to the issue of proportionality. And to bring it down to the facts which are applied in this case, one might contemplate the position of a typical sniper on the SRK side, operating from the House of the Blind, from Sharpstone, from a high-rise in Grbavica, from Baba rock. What is it that we say applies to that situation? What is the law which operates? Having regard to the wording of Article 50, it comes down to this, that the shooter who has a potential target in his sight should not shoot unless and until he can eliminate any doubt as to the status of that person. If he or she, the sniper, remains unsure, then it is unlawful to shoot. This was not a hot conflict. Here we did not have the heat of battle. Here we did not have immediate danger of being attacked, of being killed, if the sniper made a wrong call. No, here we had snipers operating from positions where they were not under attack, where they could take their time and determine whether or not a person should be targeted. There were combats during the indictment period. We've heard about the battle of Otes, Zuc, some attacks on Hum. But none of the scheduled incidents relate to those battles, those conflicts, and none of the unscheduled, the multitude of unscheduled incidents that the Prosecution has led evidence of, relate to those conflicts; only in the sense that during the battle of Zuc, for example, the accused through his subordinates would indiscriminately shell the city to bring pressure to bear on the Bosnian authorities to better his position. Mr. President, I have moved faster than I have anticipated and I have some minutes left. If there are any questions that Mr. President or Your Honours might have, then perhaps we could use the time in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, good morning. Good morning to everyone. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Defence counsel has listened to the Prosecution's final trial brief in which they have repeated their position that the evidence presented against General Galic as presented in their brief has been proved, has been supported. The counsel has presented its position on these viewpoints in its trial brief, in its final trial brief, and we shall attempt not to repeat in our verbal final trial brief what was said in our trial brief, but we will also point to other facts that support the position of the Defence according to which none of the counts in the indictment against General Galic have been proved. The Defence would like to point out that it bases its -- that the the Prosecution bases its positions on very broad assumptions and it is based on assumptions -- on conclusions reached by witnesses and not on facts, and this is not something that is allowed for by criminal law. The Prosecution has had such an approach throughout the proceedings, and this approach is manifested in its trial brief, in its final trial brief, where it has analysed, first of all, the application of the law on the basis of which the responsibility -- the criminal responsibility of General Galic should be established. And then it wants to fit some of the facts into this mould, some of the facts that the Prosecution has examined uncritically. And on the basis of such fragments, such fragmentary testimony, taken out of the testimony given by the witnesses, the Prosecution has neglected physical evidence that should have and could have been established by an analysis and by accessible written documents that the Prosecution possessed. The facts have to be proved and be supported by clear evidence, and they are not be supported by someone's conclusions and by assumptions. The only person -- the only body competent to reach decisions is the Trial Chamber, and they can base their conclusions on assumptions and conclusions of witnesses. The witnesses are here only to present facts about which they have immediate and direct knowledge, and the Trial Chamber shall reach its findings on the basis of those facts, with regard to the events and with regard to the application of law. In order for the Defence to be able to respond to the Prosecution's positions, the Defence shall follow the same sort of system in its final trial brief that the Prosecution had its in final trial brief because the Defence does not want to repeat itself and it wants to quite clearly indicate that the Prosecution's positions are absolutely erroneous and will be of no assistance to the Trial Chamber. With all due respect to the Trial Chamber, the Defence expects that the Trial Chamber, when examining the events in the Sarajevo battlefield, will first of all take into consideration the background of the conflict and this will include who first prepared for the conflict, how the conflict first broke out, how the first fighting broke out, and then it will pay special attention to establishing the fact for the scheduled incidents of sniping and shelling in Schedule 1 and 2 to the indictment. And after that, it will examine the application of the law, if on the basis of facts it is established -- whether it's possible to talk about the criminal responsibility, the legal responsibility, of General Galic, that is to say, whether such criminal responsibility exists. When presenting its positions on the application of law, in item 7 of the final trial brief presented by the Prosecution, the Prosecution supports the thesis that it is possible to convict General Galic for counts 1, 4, and 7 which it charged pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute, which is a general article -- which a general article covers, the serious violation of humanitarian law, if as the Prosecution has said in item 4, if four conditions have been met, have been satisfied. In its final trial brief, the Defence presented its positions in detail, the positions for which it does not accept the Prosecution's position and which is based on the practice of this Tribunal. It doesn't accept that Article 3 of the Statute is a general rule which covers all violations of humanitarian law which are not dealt with as crimes or contained in international customary law. The linguistic and the logical interpretation of that article, namely that Article 3 excludes that possibly because it is quite obvious that the course of the statute had in mind a special field of protection in the course of an armed conflict; namely, he had in mind physical -- material goods, physical property. The Defence wants to show that the indictment as against General Galic also charges General Galic with acts and omissions which are contained in Article 5 of the Statute. In such a case, it is not necessary with regard to these acts contained in Article 5 -- it is not necessary to refer to Article 3, even if we accepted that it would be correct to interpret these provisions of the Statute, given the attitude of the Tribunal towards this to date. The Defence's position is that Article 5 of the Statute covers all other violations of international law. The Defence would like to indicate that it is necessary to clearly distinguish Article 5 from Article 3 of the Statute because it is quite obvious that Article 3 of the Statute is intended to cover violations of the laws and customs of war. But it does not refer to physical persons, whereas Article 5 contains provisions that concern the protection of physical persons, that is to say, the protection of the civilian population. If in Article 5 there are -- if Article 5 contains crimes, mentions crimes under which the acts of the accused could be placed, then there is no justification for the Prosecution to refer to customary law and to have other offences that would be considered as crimes under Article 3 as well. In item 8, or in paragraph 8 of its final trial brief, the Prosecution provided its explanation of the unlawful infliction of terror on the civilian population and it considers that this comes under customary international law in accordance with the provisions of Article 3 of the Statute and which are -- with which one can be charged because of violating the laws and customers of war. The Defence has to point out that it is not -- it does not understand what the Prosecution wanted to claim in this part of its exposition, its presentation. Did it want to prove that these are elements of the crime of terror, or did it want to claim that these are elements that must be present if one is to establish someone's criminal possibility, elements which would constitute a crime? And thus, in paragraph 8, the Prosecution mentioned a number of elements that in the Defence's view can't constitute a crime because the element under number 5, item 8, in the Prosecution's final trial brief, that is under (e), this cannot be covered by descriptions of acts that would constitute a crime. That is, (e), which says that the accused is guilty for acts or omissions according to 7(1) or 7(3) of the Statute, Article 7(1) or 7(3). According to the Defence, one's criminal responsibility cannot be an element of a crime, cannot constitute an element of a crime. A quick analysis of the items 1 to 4. And by doing this, the Defence would like to say that perhaps the Prosecution doesn't have a clear idea of what constitutes the crime of inflicting unlawful terror on the civilian population. What does the Defence want to say? We want to say that the term "unlawful infliction of terror on civilian population" cannot contain the word, the term "unlawful." The unlawful nature of acts against civilians is a basis for treating such acts as crimes. And thus, any act that is unlawful and that violates certain values, fails to protect certain values, if it has certain social weight, it can thus be treated as a crime. If it has certain social consequences, it can thus be treated as a crime.
