utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So, before the break, the Defence started analysing the Count 1 of the indictment, paragraph 8 of the final Prosecution brief, in which the Prosecution referred to elements of the criminal offence of the unlawful infliction of terror against civilian population. It says under (a) that "the element of unlawful act is a violence." According to the Defence, the question that has to be asked, whether threat can at all constitute an element of unlawful behaviour in the condition of -- in the conditions of an armed conflict when the warring parties are making threats in relation to the operations of their units, and that question can also be phrased as to whom these threats are addressed. Now, the question can be asked whether the threats are addressed to the armed forces by their representatives of the other warring party, and it cannot be considered as being an element of the criminal offence against a civilian population. So according to the Defence, the threat would have to be made or addressed to the civilian population so that it can become part of or an element of the criminal offence of terror against civilian population. Theoretically, it is possible to envisage such a situation, that when an announcement in the media or by direct address to an unspecified number of persons that are on the side and the control of the other warring party, somebody issues a threat, and that must be considered a crime. So the threat, according to the Prosecution, is an element of a criminal offence as unlawful infliction of terror against civilian population must be issued to an unspecified number of persons. It must be serious. It must be real. And it must be capable to cause terror or spread terror among civilian population. The Defence has already stated that the unlawful nature of the acts is self-evident. But as an element of the criminal offence, all of these acts have to be specified, or at least most of them, how this terror can be caused and spread. If we look in paragraph 8, Item 3 of the final submission of Item (c) says that, "The acts of threat of violence are issued with the intention of spreading terror on the civilian population." Now, this position of the Prosecution can be acceptable in part, that when the terror is spread, acts have to be undertaken not just unlawful, but with the result of causing and spreading terror. So the intent of the perpetrator of these acts, when he undertakes these acts, must be precisely this: To cause terror or spread terror through these acts. The Defence would also like to stress that the Prosecution has insufficiently interpreted elements of the criminal offence of the unlawful causing terror to civilian population, that the Prosecution mentions or adopts in the indictment, and in further motions and submissions and positions. The Defence believes that the three proposed elements in paragraph (h) of the final Prosecution brief, which is (a), (b), and (c), elements under (a), (b), and (c), and particularly elements under (a) and (b), can only constitute two elements, because item (a) and item (b), according to the Defence, can constitute just one element of this criminal offence. While the second element of this criminal offence was proposed under item (c). These two elements under (a) and (b) that could stem from the Prosecution's position, that is unlawful violence or threat of violence to do with the infliction of terror and spread of terror among civilian population should be more specific. And pursuant to the four Geneva Conventions and Protocol II, when we are speaking about the case of the Prosecutor versus General Galic. Now the position on the application of Geneva Conventions and the additional protocols I and II, the Defence has in detail interpreted and spoken about in its final submission, and regardless of its positions referred to in the pre-trial brief where the Defence is stated that it is possible to accept that it was the obligation of the warring parties to accept all provisions of protocols I and II and the Geneva Conventions of 1949, the Defence would like to repeat that in the specific case where your Trial Chamber's decision is expected, the Protocol I should not be taken into consideration because the Protocol number I is dealing with relationships with the warring parties in international armed conflict. According to the Defence, Protocol I, that is, the provisions of Protocol I, should not be considered as legal rules because it is obvious that the Prosecutor did not prove the nature of armed conflict in the Sarajevo theatre and did not oppose the Defence's position that it is civil war that we're dealing with here, that is, an internal conflict. The Defence believes that it is groundless in this case that the Prosecution refers to Article 51 of the additional Protocol I when giving elements of the criminal offence of the unlawful terrorise -- inflicting of terror on civilians. Although in paragraph 2 of Article 51 of Protocol I, there is absolutely the same protection provided for to the civilian population as in paragraph 2 of Article 13, Protocol II, which furthers the position of the Defence that there is no place to -- that it is groundless to apply the provisions of Protocol I when we are dealing with the protection of civilian population during an internal conflict which -- that has been to be done through the application of the provisions of Protocol II of the Geneva Conventions. Now the criminal offences of the unlawful terror of civilians cannot be generalised, but they have to be specified which are the violent acts which can be undertaken with their main objective being spread of fear among civilian population. What has to be borne in mind is that the Prosecutor has not been given any guidelines of what kind of criteria, what kind of fear it should be, so that we can speak about the criminal offence of causing or spreading terror. The Defence believes that the term of "terror" must be clearly defined as an element of a criminal offence of unlawful infliction of terror on civilian population. Without this element, we cannot speak about a criminal offence. It is an element which has remained without an explanation. And according to the Defence, the Prosecutor in Count 1 of the indictment is charging General Galic for a nonexistent criminal offence. I would like to stress that the Trial Chamber's role is not to decide on what the criminal offence is. The role of the Trial Chamber is to establish certain events on the basis of facts and through assessment of evidence shown, establish whether these facts are sufficient so that they can be provided for under a certain criminal offence which has already been regulated. If it hasn't, then there is no criminal offence. When we're speaking about the charging for unlawful terror, which according to the Prosecutor General Galic has carried out through a campaign of shelling and sniping on civilian areas and civilian population, what has not been mentioned is what kind of fear must exist. What the Prosecution said, instead, was that the civilian population was that civilian population suffered from psychological suffering, and that these are the two sides of the same coin. Fear, as a psychological category, in any case is psychological suffering, mental suffering, and we cannot speak about the term of fear or causing fear, and about a separate causing of psychological suffering. Inflicting of terror as an element of a criminal offence, according to the Defence, cannot be causing of any kind of terror or causing terror of any intensity so that the fear, that is, its infliction, can be a constitutive element of a criminal offence and a significant element. It has to be of the highest intensity. It has to be long term. It has to be direct. And it has to be capable of causing long-term consequences. These four elements, when they are fulfilled, when these conditions are met, then we can speak about fear as being an element of this criminal offence. It is possible for a person to suffer from fear of high intensity, which can make this person suffer for a long time and serious consequences. And within a short period of time, a person can suffer from this kind of fear without this intensity so that it can be -- constitute an element of the criminal offence of causing terror or spreading terror. When we're speaking about fear having to last for a long time, to be a long-term condition in order to confirm the second element of the criminal offence, the way it has been envisaged by the Prosecution, which is the intent to cause fear, because otherwise, then just one act that would cause fear in another person would then bring doubt about the intent of causing fear. According to the Defence, in order to have the criminal offence of unlawful causing of terror against civilian population, what we have to establish is also the intent to cause fear or spread fear among the entire civilian population, or at least one part of the civilian population in specific conditions. When we are -- if we're dealing with a part of a civilian population against there was an intent to spread terror among them, and under this term, the Defence understands all four conditions for causing fear, as we have already explained in the previous paragraph of this final submission, then this would be a part of the civilian population that would be physically separated or these acts of infliction of violence or threats would have to be clearly defined as acts that are undertaken precisely in order to inflict terror to that -- against that part of the civilian population. In their final submission, the Prosecution under item 9 also talks of their position, that General Galic is also guilty of attacks on -- unlawful attacks on civilians under Counts 4 and 7 of the indictment in relation to Article 51 of the additional Protocol I and Article 13 of additional Protocol II, and that would be shelling or sniping, and they would be also punishable under Article 3 of the statute. This precisely here, the Defence believes that its position is justified regarding the criminal offence of unlawful infliction of terror against civilian population. The Defence states that the Prosecution has not provided enough evidence in relation to the existence of elements for the criminal offence that the Prosecution calls unlawful infliction of terror against civilian population and that the definition that has been suggested or proposed of this criminal offence by the Prosecution is not complete. Therefore, practically, this criminal offence did not exist. The Defence believes that it is necessary for acts of violence or threats of violence have to be more strictly defined. And when the Prosecution states that the acts of General Galic, there are elements and criminal offences that the Prosecution calls unlawful attacks on civilians as it is stated in Counts 4 and 7 of the indictment, although the Defence states that in the indictment there are no such words as "unlawful" but only attacks on civilians, considering the provisions mentioned of the additional protocols of the vehicles, while in the final submission the Prosecution is speaking about the unlawful attacks on civilians. The Defence has already pointed in analysing the previous case under 8 that it is unnecessary when we're speaking about the criminal offence to define it as unlawful because only an unlawful act can be considered a criminal offence. And only in certain cases is a criminal offence. What is important here is that the Prosecution should -- has been suggesting, putting forward elements of a crime that in the Defence's opinion are not acceptable because they don't point to any differences between the acts of violence and the act of threatening with violence in the elements that were suggested or put forward as the unlawful act of the infliction of terror on the civilian population in paragraph 8. It is the Defence's opinion that the Prosecution relates such acts to death or serious injuries, as in the case of -- the act of unlawfully attacking civilians. So we ask: How is it possible to commit violent acts that would not result in death or serious injury? And for those acts to represent acts that spread terror among the civilian population? In the Defence's position, terror can appear among the civilian population if the civilian population hasn't been frightened by the results that one might expect given the acts of violence. And these results would be death or serious injury. So the impossibility of making a distinction between these acts, the acts of violence that would be different in these cases, and as we said, such acts have to be specified, this impossibility doesn't allow the Prosecution to have two charges for the same act. And even less, to ask for the same of conviction that it asks in Items 1, 4, and 7 -- in Counts 1, 4, and 7 for various criminal acts that were committed through the same means, by sniping and shelling, and having the same target; namely, civilians. The Defence will now turn to paragraph 9 of the Prosecution's final trial brief, where the Prosecution suggests that the crime of unlawful attack against civilians can consist of the following, as I said in Item 9: The Prosecution said that the result of the attack was the death of civilians or the serious injury of civilians or a combination of the two; secondly, constituted by the civilian status of the population. They state that the civilian of the population or the individuals who were killed or were seriously injured was known or should have been known. They state that the attack was directed at the civilian population or at individuals. There's a connection between the attack and the armed conflict, whether it's an international or internal conflict, and the accused is criminally responsible for the attack either under Article 7(1) or 7(3) of the statute. The Defence again wants to indicate that element under (e) does not constitute a crime because one's criminal responsibility has to be established in the course of the proceedings given the acts or omissions of the person in question so that the elements suggested under (e) is not -- does not constitute a crime in the Defence's opinion. It is something that has to be established as the relation -- the attitude that an individual had towards the acts or the results of those acts. In the Defence's opinion, all four elements, the elements listed under (a) and up until (d) must be cumulatively fulfilled if they are to constitute an unlawful attack; or rather, if they are to constitute a crime. As what the Prosecution's position is in this case can be seen from the description, the analysis of the described acts, which described under Counts 4 and 7 in the indictment as unlawful attacks against civilians carried out by campaign of sniping attacks, Count 4; or by campaign of shelling civilian areas and of shelling civilian population from artillery and mortar weapons. That is stated in -- under Count 7. In both cases, the Prosecution states that General Galic is guilty of a criminal attack, an unlawful attack on civilians and divides his responsibility, treats his responsibilities on the basis of the weapons used. In the elements suggested for this crime, the Prosecution does not suggest what sort of attacks should be carried out. They only state that what is important is that there should be the intention to attack the civilian population or individual civilians, and that the result of these attacks should be the death or serious injury of civilians or a combination of these two factors. Naturally, with the condition that allows for the application of Article 5 of the statute. In the indictment, the Prosecution in Schedule 1, it has specified 24 incidents that could be representative examples as the unlawful attack on civilians -- of an unlawful attack on civilians. And the Defence would immediately like to indicate that if the acts of the accused examined with regard to the elements -- the fact that the elements of carrying out a criminal attack against a civilian have been met, then it is Defence's position that a representative example cannot be underlined in the examples put forth. All that we find are examples that have not been -- that have been proved or that have not been proved. This is a specific criminal act. An attack against the civilian population or individual civilians is carried out as stated under Item (c) of the definition put forward in Item 9 of the Prosecution's final trial brief. In such case, it is necessary to say quite clearly that each such attack, if we're talking about sniper attacks, each such attack has to be proved. It is not possible to assume that an attack was carried out against a civilian population or rather against individual civilians. It appears that in this definition the Prosecution wants to find a way in which it could support its thesis, its positions, which in the Defence's opinion can't be supported. They want to show there is an attack against the civilian population. They want to present this as a general idea, that an attack was carried out against an unspecified but a significant number of civilians. If we're talking about sniper attacks against civilians, then we can only talk about sniper attacks directed at individual civilians and not sniper attacks directed at the civilian population as a whole. Individual attacks against civilians, in the Defence's opinion, have to be proved. The Prosecution has failed to prove a significant number of individual cases, and the conclusion that the Prosecution has reached is of a general nature. In the Defence's opinion, the Prosecution has not proved intentional attacks against civilians in the 24 cases described. The element of intent when attacks were launched against a civilian population or individual civilians has to be clearly established, and it has to be proved that this was the intent, that this was decided by the person who launched the attack, and that the attack was directed against a civilian whose status was well-known or should have been well-known to the person acting. The Prosecution suggests or puts forward as an element of crime and as a significant element of crime in the case of attacks carried out against civilians, it suggests intent under (c), and the Defence accepts this. But we would like to ask how is it when describing acts in Counts 2 and 4 of the indictment, they mention the deliberate targeting of civilians from firearms, whereas under Counts 5 and 7 in the indictment, no mention is made of the intentional, the deliberate shelling of civilians. It is obvious that in the case of the criminal act carried out against civilians, the criminal shelling of civilians, the Prosecution did not refer to intent, the deliberate nature of such acts. Is seems that it extrapolates such an intent from the fact that the principle of distinction and proportionality has been violated. And in the Defence's opinion, this is something that can't be accepted. Intent has a far stronger psychological connotation than acts that some individual may take, and has a far stronger psychological connotation than the result that such an individual may desire. Far stronger than the psychological connotation that is establish when the principle of distinction and proportionality is violated. If in Count 4 of the indictment, the Prosecution referred to the deliberate targeting of civilians from firearm, the direct firing, and in Count 7, the Prosecution didn't mention the deliberate targeting of the civilian population, but only linked this to the violation of the principle of distinction and proportionality, if that is the case, this goes contrary to the idea of a criminal offence constituted by an attack against civilians, because in Item 7, there remains an essential element of a crime which is put forward by the Prosecution in paragraph 9 (c) of the Prosecution's final trial brief. In other words, there is no intent. As we said, the explanation of the principle of distinction and proportionality is, in our opinion, linked to the intent to shell. But in paragraph 10, the Prosecution -- in paragraph 10 of its final trial brief, the Prosecution states that the principle of distinction and proportionality lie at the heart of the charges for unlawful attacks. I apologise. We were referring to paragraph 10 in the Prosecution's final trial brief where it is stated that the principle of distinction and proportionality are at the heart of the charges, at the heart of the charges for unlawful attacks. The Defence will try to examine these allegations of the Prosecution and the allegations of the Prosecution in paragraph 14 of the final brief where it is stated that a large number of indiscriminate and disproportionate attacks ordered by the accused were present and they were carried out by the SRK forces that were under his command and control. And on that basis, it is possible to conclude that certain civilians, certain members of the civilian population were the subject of an attack which is contrary to Article 51, Item 2 of the protocol -- of the additional protocol and Item 13 of Protocol II. The Prosecution didn't mention what sort of attacks were carried out, and we're talking about the firearms and principle of distinction and proportionality that were violated. The Defence asks on the basis of what evidence does the Prosecution claim that General Galic ordered a significant number of indiscriminate and disproportionate attacks to be carried out? And on what basis did it then conclude that the civilian population and individual civilians were the subject of specific attacks? The principles of indiscriminate and disproportionate attacks are not related to attacks carried out against the civilian population and attacks carried out against civilian facilities because when the Prosecution presents its principle on distinction in paragraph 17 of its final trial brief, the Defence would like to say that the Prosecution had the duty to present only those items, only those items that refer to the principle of distinction. And these are items that a military commander has to respect if we're referring to the principle of distinction. These are the obligations of a military commander to direct his operations against military targets alone. In paragraph 17 of its final trial brief, the Prosecution states that attacks carried out against the categories listed below present evidence, an evidentiary basis, that the attack was directed against the civilian population, and then they mention elements listed under (a), (b), and (c). (A), as the Prosecution states, says that attacks directed against civilians as such, whether they are directed against particular targets or against civilian areas in general. (B), attacks directed at military and civilian targets without distinction. And (c), attacks directed at legitimate military targets which result in civilian victims, a number of civilian victims which is disproportionate to the military advantage that might be expected. It is immediately obvious that the sort of attacks that are described under (c) cannot by any means come under the principle of distinction because such attacks according to the Prosecution were carried out against legitimate military targets but violated the principle of proportionality and could only be categorised under the concept of proportionality. The type of attack described under (a), in the Prosecution's opinion, similarly has no connection to the principle of distinction because the Prosecution mentions attacks, describes attacks which had been deliberately directed against civilians regardless whether these attacks were directed against civilian targets or civilian areas in general. If some attack is directed deliberately against civilians, then we are no longer referring to the principle of distinction, that is to say, to the principle of distinguishing military from civilian targets because the attack is carried out with the intention of targeting a civilian object, a civilian target. The principle of distinction is only relevant in the sort of attacks that the Prosecution cites under (b) in paragraph 17 where the attacks are directed at military and civilian targets without making any distinction. The Defence has to state that the principle of distinction in the decisions taken by the competent commanders and this does not necessarily have to be General Galic in this specific case. This principle was respected to the extent that it was possible to respect such a principle under conditions of urban warfare. We believe that in the conditions of the civil war, when it is impossible to make strict distinctions between soldiers and civilians, particularly if the civilian war was unfolding in urban where in the same locations were soldiers and civilians, they were using the same facilities which was shown in evidence, in such a situation, it is absolutely impossible to fully respect the principle of distinction, that is, to use selective firing. Looking at these positions, the Defence would also like to say that in paragraph 19 of its final brief, the Prosecution's opinion is that the principle of distinction was violated on the basis of statements, that because of a presence of a person which was not protected under item -- paragraph 3 of Article 13 of the Additional Protocol II, there should not be an attack allowed against a whole group of civilians because the protection of civilian population, as the Prosecution says, would become completely illusory. Now, the Prosecution sets off from an erroneous suposition that the SRK units carried out attacks on targets where there was no clear distinction between military and civilian targets and says that it is not lawful to target civilians, only if there was a soldier present there. However, the operations of SRK units were not directed in a single case, when we are speaking about opening of direct fire, towards targets that could be both military and civilian but exclusively towards targets that were legitimate military targets. The Prosecution has not proven that there was any kind of artillery attack with direct fire that would cause victims among civilian population. The Prosecution has tried to prove that there were incidents when SRK units fired weapons for indirect shelling, that is, mortars, and that on those occasions civilians were deliberately targeted, not that these incidents happened, occurred because of the violation of the principle of distinction. In any case, the principle of distinction cannot be questioned in any of the scheduled shelling incidents because throughout the proceedings, the Prosecution has been trying to prove that these incidents occurred when civilians were deliberately targeted. In paragraphs 21 to 33, the Prosecution gave its view of the term of the principle of proportionality and saying that it was necessary for the commander to look at the situation, and according to the principle of proportionality, and according to the Prosecution, that would open up several issues. The Prosecution believes that it is not sufficient just for the commander to decide that a proposed target is a legitimate military target, but it is also necessary, as they say, to follow the time factor because some legitimate military targets do not always represent legitimate targets. Therefore, according to the Prosecutor, it is necessary to establish that the time when the decision is made there is a possibility for a partial or full destruction, taking, or neutralisation of the target in order to ensure definitive military advantage for the side undertaking the operation or the action. The Prosecutor believes that this is particularly necessary in a situation where a large number of civilians are mixed with military targets and with the dual use of facilities in urban conditions. This position of the Prosecution, this view of the Prosecution, according to the Defence, is more linked to the principle of distinction. The Prosecution believes - and the Defence believes this to be erroneous - that the principle of proportionality is in relation to the situation when it is possible to expect for a military action would cause coincidental loss of life of civilians. What also needs to be mentioned is that a commander, having decided on a legitimate military target, would expect that the opposing warring side has behaved fully according to its duties from the Geneva Conventions and that in those areas of combat operations civilians are not present, that is, civilians are not present in the area of the legitimate military target. In paragraph 23, the Prosecutor says that the principle of proportionality is contained in provisions of Article 51(5)(b) of the Additional Protocol I which prohibits indiscriminate attacks. We believe that the Prosecutor is confusing these two terms because "indiscriminate attack" means a nonselective selection of target. Therefore, we are speaking about distinction, not proportionality. Principle of proportionality is linked to the term of "ethics of warfare." As the expert of the Defence Professor Doctor Radovan Radinovic stated in his report in paragraph 235, "when there are two principles of warfare that are conflicting here, the principle of military efficiency and the principle of humaneness." According to Mr. Radinovic, the principle of military efficiency makes the commander use with maximal effect and minimal losses on their side that they would carry out their military task. The second principle, the principle is of a proper behaviour towards the enemy, which means restraining from activities that could inflict on the enemy additional suffering that would go well over the necessary force in order to neutralise the enemy and make him incapable. When we're asking the question whether anybody is acting disproportionately, then it is not a question whether anyone acted against a legitimate military target, but the question asked is whether it was necessary to use that amount of force that was used during carrying out of a military operation, military task, and achieving the necessary military success expected to be achieved by the operation undertaken. The Defence would like to cite the example of violation of the principle of proportionality during the war that the US waged in the Philippines in 1945 when Manila was taken, when there was large losses that were inflicted on the enemy personnel, 100.000 civilians were killed. And what was said is that most of them were killed during the exchange of fire. What can we say about the 253 victims during the two years' war in Sarajevo? Let us look at the example of NATO war in Yugoslavia in 1999 when there was a violation of the principle of proportionality wherewith minimal losses on their side, thousands of civilians were killed where Yugoslavia army could not be expected. In all these wars, the commanders were only bearing in mind what military objectives they had to achieve without worrying about the force used and the way this force was used, whether it was justified or not. The Defence has to stress, speaking of the question of proportionality, that it was symptomatic regarding the bombing of Television Belgrade, Wesley Clark said that we knew that the Serbian television will start working again with alternative means. There is not one single switch that would switch off everything, but we thought it was a good move to hit it and the political leadership agreed. This was his interview on TV. This target, as explained by Mr. Clark of hitting Belgrade television when 16 persons were killed, this had nothing to do with the military advantage. They didn't even try to justify the military advantage they were supposed to gain. Such examples were nonexistent in our case because the position of the Prosecutor that the SRK violated the principle of disproportionality is groundless. The Defence would like to speak about paragraph 33 of the final submission of the Prosecution, speaking about the shelling of the football match, saying that this was also one example of the violation of the principle of proportionality. Before that, the Defence would like to mention that the proportionality of an attack cannot be looked at in the light of one single incident. The Defence claims that 253 persons who were killed allegedly as a result of sniper actions as seen in the indictment is contrary to the principle of proportionality. When we're looking at other similar examples in the history of warfare, doesn't point to the violation of this principle because the military success of the SRK in combat in Sarajevo is to keep 50.000 people in this part of the theatre of operations. When I said that in paragraph 33 of their submission, the Prosecutor says that the shelling of the football match, the shelling incident number 1 from the annex number 2 of the indictment was disproportionate, we have to say that this is contrary to the claim of the Prosecutor so far that on that occasion, there was a deliberate targeting of civilians. This claim that this incident is an example of a proportional violation of the proportionality principle, the principle says that there was no military activity ongoing at that time near the football match; second, soldiers were all of low rank, it was a holiday, this was advertised, and it was probable that there would be a large number of civilians present; and under item 3, that there was no legitimate military target except for several soldiers nearby at the time of the attack. The Defence has to say that the reasons that the Prosecutor is listing to justify his position is incomprehensible, controversial, contradictory, and unacceptable. First of all, during the armed conflict when we have daily combat, it is not necessary for military action when it is undertaken; (b), absolutely caused by a military action of the opposing side from the location towards which it is operation. Now, the in the paragraph 33, the Prosecution says that the soldiers who were playing in the match, they were present there, but they were of low rank, and that that was one of the reasons that they shouldn't be allowed to have a military operation launched against them. Now if the Prosecutor says that the soldiers who were playing at the match were legitimate military target, but by respecting the principle of proportionality, this target should not be allowed because the soldiers were of low rank or because it could be expected that there would be present a large group of civilians, then the Prosecutor in this specific case needs to explain his position through the evidence shown. This -- none of the SRK members knew that there would be a match because the match was not advertised, there would have been no assumption that could be drawn that there would be a large number of civilians present because the match was played on the front line near the military targets, near the facilities of the command of the 5th Motorised Brigade. Third, now saying that there was no legitimate target near this location, apart from a few soldiers, except for the soldiers, we find this groundless, and we don't know which soldiers the Prosecution is referring to. Now, when we are speaking about the principle of proportionality, we know when there is no legitimate military target then we cannot speak about the violation of the principle of proportionality but we would have to apply a different principle in that case. When the Prosecution in Item 2 admits that the soldiers were playing a football match but they were of a low rank and that would justify the decision for them not to be targeted, but in Item 3, the Prosecution says there were only a few soldiers present nearby, not on the location during the attack. The Defence says this is a contradiction which in any case cannot be linked to the analysis of the application of the principle of proportionality. The Defence would like to stress that the Prosecution has not proven that the two mortar shells that landed on that day on the improvised football pitch from fired from the positions of the SRK units. The Defence would like to stress that the Prosecution has not come up with any exhibits, any evidence, that would confirm the operation of SRK members in a way that would be contrary to the principles of distinction and proportionality. It seems that the Prosecution wishes to use general and theoretical submissions and make the Trial Chamber conclude on the basis of certain witnesses, UNPROFOR members, that there were such attacks by SRK units; that would be nonselective, which would be a violation of the principle of distinction and proportionality. The Defence expects that the Trial Chamber on the basis of such evidence and witness testimony by Kupusovic, Mandilovic, Kovac, Mr. Tucker, Ashton, and of Mr. Baal, and for whom the Defence would like to mention they were not eyewitnesses to any of the events that would be proven here, in any of the elements regarding the deliberate attacks on civilian population, they were not eyewitnesses. The witnesses that I have listed were not questioned regarding the circumstances of the events, of every single event, of every single incident. Without that, we cannot establish that there was deliberate targeting. The Defence would like to say that in the Sarajevo theatre of operations, throughout the time relevant to the indictment, there was a daily combat that went on, which has to be looked at as a whole, because much evidence has shown that the BH army, its 1st Corps, and it took certain military actions, military operations in one part of the front with the intention to cover planned operations at the other end of the front. And in these cases as the Defence has already pointed out, it was allowed to use operations by SRK units on any part of the front against legitimate military targets in order to prevent operations of the units of the 1st Corps of the BH army. So the claims made by the witness according to which the SRK members acted in an indiscriminate way throughout the town has not been proven, and it is absolutely erroneous. In the Sarajevo battlefield -- in the part of the Sarajevo battlefield which was under the control of the 1st BH Army Corps, as the Defence expert Dr. Radovan Radinovic has stated, was an area that contained over a thousand legitimate military targets, and each action taken against such military targets were legitimate acts. And a lack of proof about civilian victims during those actions is proof that the principle of distinction and proportionality were fully respected in the course of those actions. With reference to legitimate military targets, the Defence would like to turn to a lack of understanding that our colleague Ierace mentioned with regard to the designated numbers on the map of legitimate military targets. If we have understood this correctly, our colleague, Mr. Ierace, wanted to prove that Mr. Radinovic wasn't consistent when analysing the legitimate military targets on the Sarajevo battlefield because there were numbers on the expert's map that were repeated. For example, number 47. As the Defence would like to explain that the circle containing number 47 referred to by colleague Ierace was coloured according to the key -- the colour used was according to the key, which shows that it is a combat position and the facility of units in the expected areas. That means that 47 is designated several command places in the positions of units within the brigade, and that could be the command places -- the command posts of battalions or of companies, and that is the reason for which those positions were designated by the same number, because they belonged to the same brigade. That was done in order to avoid confusion. We would like to point out that the list of legitimate military targets was compiled mostly on the basis of documents emanating from the BH army and that General Radinovic had a significant number of documents. And we would like to quote Mr. Karavelic according to which he had 30 brigades under his command. In such a case, the list of legitimate military targets and of their positions on this map would be far greater. Now, I'd like to point out that various documents have been designated with this number from the list of documents from which the expert took -- obtained information about the positions of units and their command posts, routes, bunkers, and all other legitimate military targets. The Defence would also like to turn to paragraph 34 to 37 of the Prosecution's final trial brief in which the Prosecution, in the Defence's opinion, again theoretically examines the necessity of sparing the civilian population civilian facilities, and this was something that was never disputed by the Defence. However, such theatrical considerations have no relevance to the decision reached in this case because the Prosecutor hasn't charged General Galic with unlawful acts directed against civilian facilities. And nevertheless, the Defence would like to point out that all facilities that were the subject of the attack of the SRK, of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, were legitimate military targets, or at the time when action was taken, certain operations were ongoing at that time, or the units of the 1st Corps were located in those facilities, or those facilities were used for the needs of the BH army. We would like to point out that all the buildings along the Miljacka River which were under the control of the BH army, from the post office building to the press office, from Solitara [phoen], from Momajuzair [phoen], all these high-rise buildings were legitimate military targets. Contrary to the case of the TV building being bombed by NATO in Belgrade, where there were several civilian victims, and NATO did state that the TV building was legitimate military target, the Prosecution didn't even mention and let alone prove that there were victims in the course of action taken by the SRK against the post office or the Oslobodenje building. So the only possible conclusion is the SRK units, during the fighting in the Sarjevo battlefield, did not take action against civilian areas, did not target civilian areas and civilian buildings. In paragraph 38 of its brief, the Prosecution analysed Article 5, crimes against humanity. And in items 2, 3, 5, 6, it charges General Galic with crimes as a result of unlawful attacks committed by the forces under the command of General Galic. The Prosecution claims that these attacks were carried out by snipers and by shelling, and the Prosecution says that the results of these actions were the killing of civilians and inhumane acts. In the Defence's opinion, it is obvious that the Prosecution thinks that it is sufficient to establish that an attack was carried out and that the principle of distinction and proportionality was was violated, and thus it is possible to consider such an attack as having been carried out deliberately. The Defence contests such a position. And if we are referring to the violation of the principle of distinction and proportionality, it is not possible to talk about the deliberate targeting of civilians. And if the civilians aren't the subject of a deliberate attack, there is no possibility of charging anyone with the crime of inhumane acts or murder. In paragraph 40 of its final brief, the Prosecution says that as a crime against humanity -- that murder is a crime against humanity, and this is a crime directed at General Galic under counts 2 and 5 of the indictment and it represents the unlawful and intentional killing of an individual. It put forward certain elements of the crime of murder. With regard to counts 2 and 5 in the indictment, it is obvious that causing death, killing someone, is not an act carried out by someone failing to act, by an omission. It is a matter of acting by firing from light weapons, sniping, or from heavy weapons, shelling. In this case, it was necessary for the Prosecution to show that someone was killed by sniping or shelling and to prove that that act, whether it was a sniping act or a shelling act, was committed in order to kill that person. Therefore, it is necessary to prove that the intention of the person firing was to kill the individual in question. In item 41 of its final trial brief, the Prosecution analysed counts 3 and 6, inhumane acts. In the Defence opinion, if sniping and shelling, even if the actions taken were unlawful, such actions don't violate human dignity. In item 43 to 53, the Prosecution analyses the background of the conflict. In the Defence's opinion, it misleadingly misrepresented the events in the political and social sphere of Sarajevo and the events related to the beginning of the breakout -- to the beginning of the conflict, and we believe that these allegations will be taken into account by the Trial Chamber and that the Trial Chamber will not accept the way that these events were presented by the Prosecution. In the Defence's opinion, we have presented reliable evidence on the basis of which it's possible to establish the facts concerning all the social events and the political and military actions that preceded other events and provoked the beginning of the conflict in Sarajevo, which is an area in which three peoples live. The Defence has submitted written statements, and we have also heard the oral testimony of Dr. Slavenko Terzic, Dr. Kosta Cavoski, Dr. Jelena Guskova. These were expert witnesses for the Defence who provided significant information based on reliable historical sources. And on the basis of this information, it is possible to reach the conclusions the Muslims in Sarajevo in all walks of social life, in all spheres of social life and of political life, acted in a manner that was contrary to the constitution, that violated the constitution. Much of the evidence presented in the course of these proceedings and presented before this Trial Chamber - for example, the written statements, the written statement of Dr. Radovan Radinovic - has proved -- these documents proved that the Muslims were preparing to establish their supremacy by having -- their supremacy over the Serbs and the Croats by having a recourse to war. And at the time, in order to achieve this purpose, they formed paramilitary formations. The Patriotic League was the most organised such formation, and according to the statements made by General Sefer Halilovic and General Stejpan Siber, the army was formed by the SDA, the party army, and it had been formed as early as February 1992. It is the Defence's opinion that the Muslims provoked armed conflict because they were preparing for war. We would like to support this claim of ours by referring to an article from Slobodna Bosna, dated the 27th of March, and the title was "The Bosniaks have to prepare to reach the war in Drina by having recourse to arms." The Defence doesn't want to tender this as an exhibit. I said I just wanted to use this as an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. And as I understand the course my learned colleague proposes, it is to take the Trial Chamber to a document which is not in evidence. It is not so much the document but, rather, the reference to material per se which is not in evidence to which I object. Already there have been such references in the address. But at this point, Mr. President, I make my objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, I have understood the objection. Now I'll move on to another subject. But I didn't want to tender this, to present this article as evidence. I just wanted to use this document as an example of the Muslims' position, the position of the Muslim people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Defence will indicate that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the main party's objection was not whether we see an illegible part of a newspaper on our screen, but whether it is appropriate to refer to any material which is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I just wanted to illustrate the Defence's claims. But given time restrictions, the Defence will move on to other subjects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence would like to point out that the Party of Democratic Action formed the Patriotic League and that given this position and having formed -- established an army, they demonstrated the militant nature of the SDA. We would like to say that Sarajevo is a town in which the names of institutions, squares, and streets were changed, not just institutions that had names which derived from values established during the Second World War, but also derived from the cultural and social life and that had Croatian and Serbian connotations. Before the conflict broke out, there were 160.000 Serbians living in Sarajevo, and now there are only several thousand. The Defence would like to point to a claim made by the Prosecution in paragraph 53, which is unacceptable, according to which the presentation of Milan Maudza at a meeting in May 1992 is considered to be proof that Sarajevo was at that time established as a military objective. In our opinion, that position is not acceptable not only because the Prosecution didn't refer to the source from which this document was obtained, but also because it was quite obvious that this document has manipulated by the Prosecutor because expert Donia showed it without any seals. And after the Defence had contested its authenticity in the course of the cross-examination of the Defence's witness, tried to tender as evidence a copy from the committee of -- to try to get a copy introduced as evidence which was provided by the seal from the committee of the war crimes committee from BH; and thus, the source would have been secured. It is also because the Prosecution has tried to avoid this primary source. This is the Defence Exhibit D1926. By comparing this with the primary source, Exhibit D1926 which -- whose authenticity has not been contested by the Prosecution, the secondary source and subjective information by some participant -- personal information provided by some participant, and the record from the 14th of May, 1992, these documents don't have any probative value and are undoubtedly irrelevant. The Defence would like to show the erroneous claims made by the Prosecution in paragraph 52 of its final trial brief according to which the witness Kupusovic on the 2nd of May, 1992, was the eyewitness of tanks that arrived from Lukavica and opened fire on the presidency and the town assembly. And it was stated that fire was returned from those buildings. This is a claim referred to footnote 66 where reference is made to transcript 7 -- page 718. By analysing the transcript, the Defence established that the witness Kupusovic did not claim on that page that he had seen tanks, and that the tanks came from the direction of Lukavica and that they opened fire on the presidency. The witness Kupusovic on page 718 stated that at the time, he was in Marin Dvor that he was not an eyewitness of the events referred to by the Prosecution. On page 719 of the transcript, when Mr. Kupusovic was being heard, in response to a Prosecution question as to whether certain citizens were killed in May 1992 and whether they fired from the presidency building toward the barracks and the bank, the riverbank, the witness answered that they did fire at the barracks; and in the Defence's opinion, this means that fire was opened from the presidency building, not that fire was returned, which is what the Prosecution would have us believe. And it is not correct to state in the transcript of Mr. Kupusovic that the tanks came from Lukavica and opened fire on the presidency. In its final brief, the Prosecution is also looking from 54 to 61 at the pattern of sniping and shelling of the areas held by the BH army. The definition according to the Defence that's adopted by the Prosecution in order to describe the nature of this case cannot be accepted. What the Prosecutor claims, that the international military personnel stationed in Bosnia also adopted the same meaning as the Prosecution has. This is to do with Witness Indic in footnote 69 of the final brief that the sniper cannot be defined as the Prosecution has defined it. The Prosecution claims that it has no consequence, that the term of "sniping" the way they are treating it is different from the usual military meaning, and this is unacceptable. First of all, the reason for the existence of snipers in an army is precisely to have specific tasks; and to eliminate snipers on the other side. As a rule, this is done from a longer distance. And that's why it's important to accept that an important element of sniping is the actual weapon that is fired. This weapon has to have an optical sight because absolute precision is required. The Defence further claims that in the final submission, it is unacceptable to say that the SRK soldiers had rifles that had optical sights. The claim of the Prosecution speaking of a witness that allegedly said that this person had seen a rifle with an optical sight cannot be accepted as proving that SRK units had these rifles. Further on in the submission, 54 to 60, it is not possible to see what the Prosecution's position is regarding the pattern of shelling of town areas because it would be concluded that the sniping was constant. But the -- it is not clear whether the Prosecution believes that the exchange of fire in any case is sniping. If this is so, then this position is thoroughly erroneous, because if the Prosecutor believes that the SRK soldiers were firing at random on the city and sniping, and that would be even less acceptable, particularly when there are claims that criminal offences of murder were committed, or inhumane acts that were not murder. Since the Prosecutor himself said that this had to be done deliberately, with intent, while if we have random shooting, the intent is excluded. As the Prosecutor cited yesterday, the sniping incident of case of are Rasid Dzonko. The Prosecution wants to show that there was a pattern of shelling. In order to establish this pattern speaks about the testimony of Witness Mandilovic and Kupusovic. And in paragraphs 56 and 57 is speaking precisely about the statements of the testimonies of the witnesses heard before this Chamber. The Prosecution is also speaking about the testimony of Colonel Cutler and Colonel Mole and Mr. Baal. By analysing carefully what the witnesses said, the Defence believes that a completely different conclusion can be reached, contrary to the one that the Prosecution wishes to impose. If Witness Mole says that not a single day passed quietly without shelling, then according to the Defence, it is obvious that combat was ongoing. And during one period of time, they were more intense; and during another period of time, they were less intense. But in any case, it can be concluded that the cease-fires that were agreed upon were not respected. All of these witnesses that I have listed and that the Prosecution mentions and speak about them, they said that there was a daily shooting. The Defence would like to stress that testimony of these witnesses and all the other witnesses spoke about deliberate targeting of witnesses, civilian facilities, for instance, Witness Ashton. Can that be a basis for reaching the conclusion that there was indeed deliberate targeting of civilians? Because they all form the same conclusions but they did not describe a single incident where they would explain a location where this happened, describe a victim or victims, describe the location where the projectile was fired from. So that on the basis of all of this data, one could conclude whether this was correctly concluded or not. So these generalised claims of the witnesses that there was shooting in town without the witnesses listing, citing locations where the shells landed, grenades landed, where the projectiles ended up, fired from firearms, are of little assistance to establish facts in order to assess whether there was deliberate targeting of civilians or whether civilians were threatened or at risk because of the violation of principles of distinction of proportionality. The Prosecutor neglecting the fact that Sarajevo is only that part of town which is represented by the old town at Bascarsija, going towards -- west to Alipasino Polje, Dobrinja, while the areas of Zuc, Hum, Pofalici, Vogosca, Ilidza, Lukavica, and Hadzici, the Prosecutor is excluding these areas from the town. The Defence is mentioning this because the exhibit -- the evidence was shown, and this was also explained in the report of Mr. Radinovic, that the Prosecution erroneously made up a thesis that SRK units were on the dominant high elevations around Sarajevo. The Defence evidence was that the fire from the positions of the SRK was only opened as responding to fire. It was only opened because of firing by the 1st Corps of the BH army. What Defence has to say is that the units of the 1st Corps of the BH, they were the ones that from the very start of the conflict, or immediately after the conflict started, they were the ones that held all the high positions in Sarajevo, Zuc hill, Hum, Brijesko Brdo, Sokolje, Mojmilo. They were even on the slopes of Trebevic, on the elevations of Debelo Brdo, Mala, and Velika Colina Kapa, and in the area of Sedam Suma and Grdonj. I would also like to stress that the forces of the 1st corps of the BH army in the actual town had the highest towns -- highest buildings in the town which is the executive council, the business premises of UNIS, and Energoinvest. We believe that we have analysed the evidence thoroughly in the final submission and Defence does not wish to repeat itself.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.
