utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...words again. You saw me looking at the clock, if you would find a suitable moment to -- for a break, please indicate so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence just wishes to mention the witnesses mentioned by the Prosecution who spoke about the daily shelling and sniping. We wish to say that they were not telling the full truth -- the whole truth. There were -- they gave a direct assessment of the exchange of fire and operations. If it is true that at some intervals, there were intense shelling, which the Defence does not contest, we would like to point out that these were not acts of shelling towards the town as this was concluded by the witnesses or mentioned by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. We'll adjourn, and we'll resume in 20 minutes, at 10 minutes to 10.00 [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before the break, we were speaking about the intensity of shelling and the assessing the witness testimony, the witnesses mentioned by the Prosecution's brief. The Defence would like to say that also, the Prosecution referred to -- in paragraph 59 referred to the testimony of witness Cutler about the intensity of firing. What we have to bear in mind is that in December there was intense combat ongoing for Otes, and at that time, BH army forces during that period periodically tried to break through the line of defence of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And their intention was this line should have to be broken towards Ilidza. The evidence was demonstrated that there was constant combat in the Sarajevo battlefield, so it's a normal conclusion that there was no pattern of sniping or shelling as the Prosecutor wishes to show. In its final submission, the Prosecution also refers to whether there was direct evidence on the criminal responsibility of General Galic. Now, in paragraphs 82 to 91 of the final brief, the Prosecution is dealing with direct responsibility of General Galic, according to the provisions under Article 7, Item 1 of the statute. The position of the Prosecution is unacceptable for the Defence. The Prosecution claim that the Prosecution witnesses expressed contrary testimony to the witnesses of the Defence. This was to do with the experienced journalist, Witness AD, UNPROFOR witnesses, and they say that these are reliable witnesses and they have to be believed. As far as witnesses AD and D are concerned --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I be heard in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. When the Prosecution refers to the military personnel of the UN, we would first of all like to point out that the Prosecution didn't mention which witnesses, which UN members, spoke about the facts referred to by the Prosecution about the information that they had - and the Prosecution mentions it in paragraphs 82 and 91 - about the information they had about trained snipers, about sniper rifles or sniper nests, sniper positions in the SRK. The Defence claims that individual witnesses, UN members, for example, such as General Razek or Witness WV, were not telling the truth, especially in the parts of their testimony that they gave before the Trial Chamber because the statements given by those witnesses contradict the statements that the witnesses gave to investigators from the OTP, the Office of the Prosecution. It is the Defence's position that not a single witness had information -- had direct information about how the members of the SRK were armed, nor did anyone confirm that there were snipers with professional sniper rifles within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The allegation of the Prosecution that as far as the professional sniping rifle is concerned, that it's not necessary for such a rifle to have an optical sight, in the Defence's opinion this position is unacceptable. According to the stories that there were -- that there was sniping activity, as alleged by the Prosecution, it's not possible to establish from where they took action, who acted, and against whom they acted. The Defence would like to point out, and you, Your Honour, also mentioned this in response to the Defence's motion for acquittal, when you established that in three cases the Prosecution did not provide evidence on the basis of which one could come to the conclusion and to establish beyond any reasonable doubt that civilians were deliberately targeted from the positions of the SRK units. And this is why the Defence is again repeating that the Prosecution cannot claim with regard to any single incident - and we don't even know whether such incidents occurred - they can't claim that such incidents with the intention of targeting civilians and that the SRK or members of the SRK acted with such intent. Now, the Defence would also like to add that in addition to the fact that General Galic, after having assumed his post, managed to an extent to ensure that all the units in the zone of the SRK were under the command of the SRK, in spite of the fact that he managed -- in addition to the fact that he managed to do this, there is the fact that -- it is a fact that control was effectively established. However, perhaps he did not succeed in fully establishing such control because given the size of the front, it was possible for individuals to act outside the practical and theoretical control of the SRK command. And thus, the Prosecution with regard to the direct responsibility of General Galic has not provided sufficient evidence that would bear out such criminal responsibility of the accused. The Prosecution also claims that on the basis of protests that were personally submitted to General Galic, either through liaison officers or through officers at other positions, together with evidence, as the Prosecution says, or as admitted or as admitted by other subordinates, it claims that operations were continued in spite of the protest that had been lodged. We would like to point out - and this is something that we said in our final trial brief - we would like to point out that General Galic never personally received a protest and he didn't receive any protests through subordinate officers either with regard to any deliberate sniping of civilians. Not a single Prosecution witness supported such claims made by the Prosecution. And with regard to the Witness General Razek and Witness VV, with regard to their statements that General Galic said that the Muslims had to be destroyed, these allegations are incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's the same complaint as made previously in relation to a different witness, the same reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but I think that we spoke about this witness yesterday, and that we weren't in private session. I think that the Prosecution also referred to the testimony of this witness. But I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not clear in my mind. But even if that would be the case, then the Prosecution would deserve to be reprimanded, if that would be the case, but that would not entitle the Defence to continue that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would prefer now to go in private session for a while?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, I won't refer to him within that context. I won't mention the initials. I will inform the Trial Chamber when I reach the subject. The Defence would like to point out that General Galic did not receive a single protest from anyone, and I would like to repeat this yet again, not a single protest regarding particular sniping incidents. And this means that there was no possibility of conducting any sort of investigation into a given incident that occurred in the territory under the control of the enemy side. We would also like to point out that the BH army organs weren't informed about the incidents of the alleged snipers, of the alleged sniper activity. And if they weren't informed of such events - and this has been borne out by the evidence - then the UN representatives weren't informed of them either. Not a single witness who was a UN member testified about being aware of any kind of protest being sent to the SRK command and that concerned individual sniping events. I have to point out that such questions were put to all the witnesses by the Defence, to all the UNPROFOR members who testified before this Trial Chamber. The Defence would also like to remind the Trial Chamber that the evidence shows that from the corps commander and right down to the lowest command of military units within the SRK - so from brigade commanders, battalion commanders, company platoon commanders, detachment commanders - we're referring to this chain of command, and we are claiming that each of these commanders at each level was obliged to inform his superiors, and this means that soldiers, first of all, had to inform the commanders of detachments, and then the commander of detachment would have to inform the commander of platoon, and the information would have to be relayed further up the scale in that manner. What we're trying to say is that the corps commander cannot establish control of each and every soldier. Even less is it possible for each commander in the chain of command to be aware of what a given soldier may have done, of what sort of acts a certain soldier may have committed at the front line. If we assume that he was involved in sniping, he will never admit to his commander that he killed civilians, and all witnesses for the Defence who were soldiers at the front line have confirmed that according to the orders they received it was strictly forbidden for them to target civilians. Even if a soldier fired at a civilian, he would remain silent about that fact, in spite of the fact that he may not even have been in a position to know whether he had hit someone on the other side. If he was sure he had hit someone, would he inform someone of this? And if there was an order according to which civilians should not be targeted, then it would be clear to such a soldier that he would be punished. This is why such soldiers remain silent, and no one within the chain of command, and especially not on the sixth level of command, no one was informed of such an incident and could not even have assumed that such acts occurred. The evidence presented by the Defence has proved that in cases of -- some cases of shelling, General Galic ordered investigations to be carried out. And DP35, the Defence witness, confirmed that the investigations carried out showed that SRK units in those particular cases were not involved. They were not involved in those cases. When the Prosecution referred to the evidence and the testimony of General Rose according to which not only generals but also politicians in military discussions doesn't have any importance, and this can only show that to a certain extent, politics got involved in the system of command. And General Radovan Radinovic has spoken about the difficulties that Galic had in establishing SRK command. He spoke about the -- he mentioned this in his written statement. We would like to point out that the Prosecution has not proven that General Galic ordered sniper action of any kind directed against civilians. The Prosecution hasn't proved that any of his acts encouraged or assisted attacks against such civilians. They didn't prove that he was informed about a single incident. And in the Defence's opinion, the way in which General Galic behaved - who as we have already said is a highly moral person and soldier - there were no omissions or actions for which he would have to bear direct criminal responsibility. The allegations of the Prosecution set forth in paragraph 90, according to which the direct criminal responsibility is proven, has no foundation. As we have just said, it hasn't been proved that General Galic participated in any way in any event in which snipers deliberately targeted civilians. The Prosecution in its final trial brief has also mentioned the command responsibility of General Galic pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute. In its final trial brief, the Defence has analysed each individual incident, both of sniping and of shelling, in detail. And in our final trial brief, we have indicated that there is no evidence that could be used to establish the guilt of any member of the SRK because quite simply there was no evidence to prove that in any of the scheduled incidents referred to by the Prosecution, in none of that evidence was it established that civilians were deliberately targeted or that action was taken that violated the principle of distinction and proportionality. In paragraph 92 of its final trial brief, the Prosecution has mixed up certain ideas, either intentionally or unintentionally. First of all, there was no evidence that would show that any organisation of the SRK, there was a high level of command and control over subordinate units. But even if there were units or individuals who were out of control, the Defence didn't present evidence that such individuals would have targeted civilians and not individuals under the command of the SRK. The Prosecution is claiming that the witness -- the witnesses for the Defence have established the chain of command. This is not in dispute. The Defence has proved this through witnesses just to help the Trial Chamber to see that the level of command that the lowest units had right up to the command of the SRK. And to show that each commander was held responsible for the military tasks that that commander performed. This was not for the Defence to prove, that there were elements that did not fit into that chain of command. On the contrary, the Defence tried to provide evidence that would prove that General Galic took all measures for the SRK units to respect that command after he had assumed command of these units. General Galic, as we said in our final trial brief, he succeeded in doing this to a great extent with respect to individual paramilitary formations that appeared in the zone under the control of the SRK. There were many cases and the Defence expert General Radovan Radinovic has also spoken about this. And in the documents disclosed, documents that the Defence hasn't been able to present to the Trial Chamber, not all of them, on that basis, it's possible to see to what extent General Galic strove to place all units under the command of the SRK. And it has also shown how difficult it is. Certain units were even disbanded, some individuals were arrested and criminally prosecuted, too. When General Galic assumed the position of commander, it doesn't mean that there weren't groups or individuals who functioned outside the chain of command. We would in particular like to point out that the front was 237 kilometres long and had a surface of over 2.000 square kilometres. Naturally, the Defence did not try to prove that such groups or individuals from such groups targeted civilians, because it wasn't necessary since the Prosecution only provided evidence for the so-called scheduled incidents. So the Defence concentrated on obtaining evidence, on presenting evidence to contest the allegations made by the Prosecution. The Defence would like to point out, and this is borne out by the evidence, that not a single event were civilians deliberately targeted from the divisions of the SRK. Evidence hasn't shown where the projectiles came from, if we are referring to firearms, or where the shells came from if we are talking about mortars. And it is quite clear that it would be pointless to try and prove all the elements of -- the criminal and legal responsibility of General Galic which should be supported if he is to be held accountable on the basis of command responsibility for the acts committed by his subordinates. In other words, we want to show that if in the incidents referred to, it hasn't been shown that there were incidents of shelling or sniping. If it hasn't been shown that a single individual from the SRK participated in such acts and if the deliberate targeting of civilians hasn't been proven in the case of the incidents cited, then likewise, the illegal unlawful conduct of someone from the SRK hasn't been proven. And thus, the criminal responsibility of General Galic for such acts has not been proven either. The Prosecution in its final trial brief admits that it hasn't been proven beyond any reasonable doubt that the superior command, the main staff, ordered the corps command to take any kind of action against civilians. And thus, it is obvious that we can't talk about the planning of such actions. Even if individual incidents had been proven, but they haven't been proven, there should be reports from lower commands about these incidents, reports to the brigade command should have information about individual incidents in which there was unlawful targeting of civilians so that in this manner, General Galic could be informed of the event, if any. The exhibits of the Defence attached to the statement -- to the report, rather, of Mr. Radinovic, and exhibits of the Defence that were shown through the witness Milorad Bukva, DP34, DP14, and all the other documents of the SRK command that the Defence disclosed to the Prosecutor, and as I said, we are not in a position to tender each and every single one of these documents as evidence, they clearly show that not a single report to the command of the brigades had any data regarding possible incidents that occurred unlawfully. And this demonstrates that General Galic who received such reports was not informed about any incident that would require him to launch an investigation regarding this incident. The Defence claims that General Galic always ordered launching of an investigation regarding the incidents he was informed about. Now, regarding the exhibits of the Defence attached to the report of Dr. Radinovic, these are 260, 254, D255, and D248, the results of the investigations were that there were no omissions in the way the SRK units operated. The Defence has already pointed out that the Prosecution witnesses who were members of UNPROFOR -- had been members of UNPROFOR did not establish the existence of any protests regarding individual incidents, of scheduled incidents, of sniping. The Defence has already spoken about this, and this is included in the final brief, and we will speak more later about the shelling incidents. Specifically, about the claims of the Prosecution there were many incidents, sniping or shelling incidents, that were not included in the annexes of the indictment 1 and 2. This is a claim that is groundless, according to the Defence, and it cannot even be discussed, particularly no evidence can be shown in relation to such events. The Prosecutor claims that General Galic ordered attacks against civilians. And he uses circumstantial evidence for this which is unacceptable according to the Defence. We have said -- we stated that General Galic, that it has not proven that General Galic had ordered any kind of attacks against civilians. It has not been proven that General Galic knew or had reason to know that his subordinates had carried out such acts. That would be considered as criminal offences under the Article 2(2)(v) of the Statute. As the Defence witnesses claim, General Galic stated explicitly that civilians should not be targeted, and he had no specific information that anything like that had occurred except in the already described incidents of shelling when an investigation was launched and the Defence had cited which Defence exhibits relate to this which point to the existence of an investigation in relation to some information that there was some shelling. And the investigations were launched by General Galic. The Defence further would like to point that if General Galic had not known that some incidents had happened, then he couldn't have any measures undertaken to punish anyone for these incidents or to prevent the repetition of such incidents, although we reiterate, and this was stressed by the Defence witnesses, there were orders issued constantly about the protection -- about the respective Geneva Conventions not to target civilians, and this was also mentioned by DP 5, DP 11, and other witnesses of the Defence who were soldiers on the front line. Defence would also like to stress something that we do not contest, that the way that the SRK was involved in the conflict against the BH army. There was a high degree of organisation that was reached in the SRK. But Defence does not understand why this is so important for the Prosecution regarding the communication. When we are speaking about specific incidents, we know that General Galic did not have such information. And the Prosecution referring to General -- to Lieutenant-Colonel van Baal, and this is in paragraph 100 of the final brief, and 101 regarding Colonel Mole or paragraph 102 or 103 regarding Colonel Gardemeister. They are irrelevant because it is not confirmed that General Galic had any information about any incidents. Also, the Defence is also aware that the Prosecution is also speaking about the testimony of Witness Tucker regarding the system of communications, the general system of communications which mentions that General Mladic would have to speak to someone in order to find something out, and that was happening quickly. And the Defence asked the question: What is the connection between General Galic with the communication system that General Galic had with his subordinates? Because if an army is well organised, that General Mladic primarily was supposed to receive information from General Galic. Under paragraph 106 of the final brief, the Prosecutor says that Witness Indic said that each brigade had their own artillery group, and that the use of the artillery was within the remit of the brigade command. All the orders as a principle was issued by the brigade commander. Such an order would then be logged in the report which is submitted to the corps command. The Defence do not contest such statements of Witness Indic because the chain of command precisely was as Witness Indic described it. In paragraph 105, the Prosecution relies on the testimony of Witness Carswell. But before I start analysing the paragraph 105, we would like to point out that in paragraph 106 regarding the testimony of Witness Indic, in fact, it is the Defence's claim which is supported here that General Galic did not issue orders to units that were part of the brigade but he issued orders, commands, written orders to the brigade commanders, and they then later in their commands processed them and forwarded their own orders to commanders of other units, to company commanders, their own orders. So -- and this is what the Defence wish to say regarding paragraph 106 of the Prosecution final brief. We have said, the Defence has said that paragraph 105 of the Prosecution final brief, the Prosecution spoke of the testimony of Witness Carswell about how the artillery command was carried out and how lists and plans of targets were made. The Defence can accept that there was a scheme, there was a plan and lists of targets. But we would like to point out immediately that these schemes, plans, target lists were made up only in relation to legitimate military targets. Only if among the lists, there were also facilities that before the war had been civilian facilities and which before the conflict broke out had the status of civilian buildings, civilian facilities, and we have seen from the evidence that the Defence offered to the Trial Chamber, we know that we have seen in such buildings that had the status of civilian buildings, there were troops that were stationed, equipment, ammunition, and other items necessary for military. So these buildings would be executive council, Hrasnica, Zenica, Vasa Miskin factory, and so on. These buildings were mentioned many times in this courtroom. So the Prosecutor never proved the unlawful nature of the SRK units' acts, nor did the Prosecutor prove that General Galic ever issued any unlawful orders. It was not proved that General Galic -- it was not proved that there were such firing and that General Galic could have known about them. And if he hadn't done anything to prevent such behaviour, if he hadn't known but found out later and did not do anything to punish those who had carried out illegitimate orders. And therefore, there is no criminal legal responsibility regarding General Galic. Now, the Defence would like to say a few words about the claims of the Prosecution that General Galic's subordinates had targeted civilians. This is dealt with in paragraphs 107 to 128 of the final brief of the Prosecution. Now, the Defence would like to speak about the testimony about the witness who was protected. I would ask if we can go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session, I think, would be sufficient, if you're just speaking about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you. If the position of the Prosecution is that through his testimony it has been proven that the witness was speaking about the snipers firing at civilians, the Defence would like to state here that this position is unacceptable. First of all, this witness said that there were units -- there were snipers in other units. He didn't mention which units these were. Also, this part of the testimony of Witness D is contradictory with his more general testimony. He said that occasionally, snipers joined his unit, and he said he very frequently heard firing, and he also said that he frequently spoke to them. So what does that mean, "very frequently"? When he said that they occasionally came, also, if it's very frequently, then that would mean that he frequently spoke to them or he occasionally spoke to them. The witness also said that during those rare moments, they told him that they had fired into an area where there were civilians, but he had also said -- or he said that he wasn't sure whether he had actually hit anyone. Now, whether they had hit anyone, that is not proof that they had actually hit somebody; occasional arrival of snipers who would come according to the Defence. That means they would appear only when they were needed to target their snipers on the other side, those that were located on Holiday Inn hotel. And now, when the witness mentioned M76 rifle that the witness described, the Defence would like to state that when we look at witness testimony of DP30, certainly the one who knows about the equipment and weapons, he would know whether this equipment was in existence in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Also, we will speak about the Witness D whose testimony states that he often saw mortars fire or shell Radnicka Street. And he said that they were frequently intoxicated, they were not able to fire. This is contradictory to Witness Carswell, Gardemeister, Prosecution witnesses, in relation to 103, 104 paragraphs in the Prosecution final brief who have stated that the SRK members who were on their firing positions were very efficient and very professional. So what this witness said, and the Prosecution wishes to admit his testimony, that snipers had confirmed to him that they were firing at people on crossroads where there were containers, that he had seen this, this cannot be taken as truth, that this was targeting civilians because this was done in order to protect the soldiers in those parts of the city where the demarcation lines were very close. Your Honours, bearing in mind the time...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd find this a suitable to --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In a very global way, I calculate the time still available, that would be 2 and a half hours for the Defence tomorrow approximately. I'll check with Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.
